analysis.one_liner: Bans ultraprocessed foods and specific chemical additives from school lunches.
analysis.headline: The bill to strip ultraprocessed foods and certain food dyes from school lunches has been referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has received no further action since its April 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the National School Lunch Program's nutrition rules so that schools cannot serve ultraprocessed foods — as defined by a standard food-classification system — or foods containing potassium bromate, propylparaben, titanium dioxide, brominated vegetable oil, or eight specific synthetic food dyes. Millions of children eat lunches under this federal program every school day, so the change would directly affect what is on their trays. It was introduced by a single Republican representative with no cosponsors and referred to committee, where no action has been taken. [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 30 million children who eat lunches through the National School Lunch Program, most from lower-income households, would get meals free of ultraprocessed foods and several additives that health advocates have flagged, including eight synthetic dyes. Parents and school nutrition staff who want simpler, whole-food meals also benefit from a clear federal standard. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Kids in the federal school lunch program

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a requirement to the school lunch program's minimum nutrition standards that menus prohibit ultraprocessed foods, defined as group 4 of the NOVA classification system, a widely used research category covering industrially formulated products. [S3]

It also prohibits foods containing potassium bromate, propylparaben, titanium dioxide, brominated vegetable oil, and eight synthetic dyes (yellow 5, yellow 6, blue 1, blue 2, green 3, red 3, red 40), several of which are already banned or restricted elsewhere or are being phased out under separate FDA actions. [S2] [S3]

Because these standards apply to every school participating in the National School Lunch Program, the rule would reach meals served to tens of millions of children nationwide, the majority of them from low- and moderate-income families. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage manufacturers would bear the cost of reformulating products or losing school-lunch sales, and school districts would face the work and expense of finding compliant suppliers and adjusting menus. If compliant whole foods cost more than processed items, schools may need additional funding to absorb the difference. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Processed food makers and school districts

drawbacks.text: The ban covers a very broad category — all ultraprocessed foods under the NOVA group 4 definition — which includes many everyday items such as whole-grain breads, yogurts, and cereals that nutrition experts generally consider healthy, so schools could lose access to affordable staples without a clear substitute. [S3]

The bill provides no additional funding for schools to pay for reformulated or whole-food alternatives, so districts could face higher food costs at a time when school meal budgets are already tight. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Removing several specific additives from school meals has a solid case behind it and would be a manageable change for food makers. The blanket ultraprocessed-food ban is the harder part: the NOVA category is broad, drawing the line between compliant and banned foods will be contentious, and without new funding the cost falls on school food budgets. The specific-additive bans are the easier win; the ultraprocessed-food prohibition would need careful definitions and money behind it to work without disrupting meal programs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2025 with no cosponsors and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no floor action. [S4] [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Kennedy (R-UT) introduced the Healthy Lunch for Healthy Kids Act on April 1, 2025. [S1] [S5]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, and no further action has been recorded since. [S5]
No other member of the House has signed on as a cosponsor. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has changed position: processed-food makers keep selling to schools unchanged, and children's meals stay as they are. With no cosponsors and no committee action, the bill's backers have gained a record of the idea but nothing more. Short: "No one yet; the bill has not moved."

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill has not moved

for.name: Rep. Mike Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee; no cosponsors joined. [S1] [S4] [S5]

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 1, 2025 and has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and there are no cosponsors, so there is no record of partisan alignment; the sponsor is a Republican with no Democratic or Republican cosponsors listed. [S4]

industries.note: The bill would ban their products — ultraprocessed foods and foods containing specific additives and dyes — from the school lunch market, forcing reformulation or loss of sales. Children eating those meals would get simpler, additive-free food. [S2] [S3]
Suppliers of potassium bromate, propylparaben, titanium dioxide, brominated vegetable oil, and synthetic dyes would lose a slice of demand as school meals phase the ingredients out. [S2] [S3]
Districts and their suppliers would need to source compliant foods and rework menus, adding cost and administrative work in the short run, while serving cleaner meals to students. [S3]

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action eight months after introduction, the bill is unlikely to advance. Most single-sponsor bills referred to committee without cosponsors die quietly at the end of the two-year Congress unless the sponsor builds support or leadership takes interest.
